text: A kettle left to boil on a gas ring uses more fuel than an electric one filled to the right level.

Bread keeps longest in a cloth bag at room temperature. In the fridge the crumb turns dry within a day, although mould arrives later. A stale loaf is not lost: sliced and toasted it serves for another two mornings, and the last crusts can be dried in the oven and grated over baked dishes.
The morning bus on the ring road is fullest between half past seven and eight. Passengers who can leave ten minutes earlier usually find a seat.

Wool jumpers should be washed in cool water with very little soap and never wrung out. Press the water out between two towels, pull the garment gently back into shape and let it dry flat, away from the radiator. Hung on a line, the wet wool stretches under its own weight and the sleeves end up a hand longer than before.
Tomato plants on a balcony need water every evening in July and a stick to lean on.

A bicycle chain that squeaks is asking for oil. Wipe the old grime off with a rag first, then put one drop on each link while turning the pedals backwards. Too much oil collects dust, so wipe the chain once more when you are done.
Most household dust is made of fibres from clothes and carpets, mixed with soil carried in on shoes. A doormat on each side of the front door stops more of it than any amount of sweeping later.
When the clocks go back in autumn, the dog still wakes at the old time. For about a week the household is walked an hour early, until habit catches up with the calendar.
Rain on a tin roof sounds heavier than it is, which is why garden sheds feel so cosy.

Soup tastes better on the second day because the flavours have had time to settle. Cool the pot quickly, keep it covered in the fridge and bring it to a full boil before serving again. Soups with pasta are the exception, since the pasta keeps soaking up liquid and turns soft.
A drawer that sticks in damp weather can be eased by rubbing a candle stub along its runners. The wax fills the grain of the wood and lets the drawer slide for several months.
Parking near the weekly swimming lesson is easiest on the far side of the sports hall, where the spaces are wider and few drivers bother to look.

Houseplants suffer more from too much water than from too little. Before watering, push a finger into the soil up to the second knuckle. If it comes out dry, water until a little runs into the saucer. If it comes out damp, wait another two days and test again.
The corner shop sells stamps, bus tickets and string, and closes for lunch from one until two.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, because it cuts where you aim it and needs less force. Ten strokes on a steel before each use keep the edge, and a whetstone twice a year restores it.

On washing day the line in the yard fills in a fixed order: sheets at the back where the wind is strongest, shirts in the middle, socks at the front within easy reach. The pegs live in an old biscuit tin with a hole punched in the bottom to let the rain out.
Cats decide for themselves which chair is theirs. Moving the cat settles nothing, since it returns as soon as the seat is free.
The first frost usually arrives in the last week of October. Gardeners lift the dahlias the day after, cut the stems down to a hand's width and store the tubers in dry sand in the cellar until April.
Left in a warm car, chocolate melts within twenty minutes and sets again with a pale bloom.
A letter posted before the evening collection reaches most addresses in the country the next working day. Parcels take two days, and anything sent on a Friday afternoon rarely moves before Monday.
The stairwell light runs on a timer of three minutes, which is just enough to reach the fourth floor with two bags of shopping, provided nobody stops to talk on the second.
Pancake batter improves if it rests for half an hour before it meets the pan.

Shoes dry best stuffed with newspaper and left near, not on, a source of heat. Change the paper after an hour. Leather that dries too fast cracks along the creases, and no polish will close those lines again.
The weather forecast for the coast is read out at ten to six each morning. Fishing boats and dog walkers listen for the same two things: the direction of the wind and the hour of high water.
Children learn to tie their laces at about six. Until then, a double knot tied by an adult in the morning usually lasts until the afternoon.

To clean a window without streaks, wash it with warm water and a drop of washing-up liquid, then dry it with crumpled newspaper. Choose a cloudy day. In direct sun the water dries before you can wipe it and leaves marks that only show when the light comes in low the next morning.
Onions keep for months in a net hung somewhere cool, dark and dry.
The queue at the post office is shortest just after it opens and longest at lunchtime on the last day of the month, when the rent, the pensions and the parcels all arrive together.
A squeaking door hinge needs one drop of oil at the top of the pin. Swing the door a few times to work it in and wipe away what runs down.

Rice cooks evenly when the lid stays on. Use one cup of rice to one and a half cups of water, bring it to the boil, turn the heat as low as it goes and leave it alone for twelve minutes. Then take the pan off the heat and wait another five before lifting the lid.
On the allotments, water comes from a shared tap that is turned off in November. Anyone who forgets to drain their hose before then finds it split by spring.
A wet umbrella belongs in the stand by the door, never open on the hallway floor.
The walk to school takes eleven minutes at an adult's pace and nineteen with a child who has noticed a snail. Leaving at ten past eight allows for one snail and one puddle.
Most smoke alarms chirp when the battery runs low, and they nearly always start at night. Keeping a spare battery in the kitchen drawer turns a lost hour of sleep into a job of two minutes.
Coffee grounds can go on the compost heap along with the paper filter. Worms like them, and the heap smells less sour in summer when a handful is mixed in each day.

A suitcase packs best with shoes along the hinge side, heavy things at the bottom when it stands upright, and shirts rolled, not folded. Leave a corner free for whatever comes back that did not go out.
The library is quietest on weekday mornings, when the reading room smells of floor polish.

Paint for a small room is easy to work out. Measure the walls, subtract the door and the window, and allow one litre for every ten square metres per coat. Two coats are almost always needed, and a dark old colour under a pale new one needs three.
The evening train stops at every station after nine o'clock. A journey that takes forty minutes at noon takes a full hour, and the buffet car is closed.
Eggs straight from the fridge crack when dropped into boiling water. Let them stand on the counter for a quarter of an hour first, or start them in cold water and count from the moment it boils.
Lawn grass grows fastest in May. Mowing once a week at a medium height keeps it thick enough to crowd out moss, and the clippings can be left where they fall as long as they are short.
Keys left in the door on the inside stop the lock from being opened from the hallway.

A good stock begins with bones roasted until they are brown. Cover them with cold water, add an onion, a carrot, a stick of celery and a few peppercorns, and let the pot barely tremble for three hours. Skim the surface now and then. Salt goes in at the very end, once the liquid has been strained and reduced.
The lift in the block is checked on the first Tuesday of every month, between nine and eleven. On those mornings the residents of the upper floors do their shopping the day before.
Candles burn evenly if the wick is trimmed to the width of a fingernail before lighting.

Wooden chopping boards last for years if they are washed by hand and left to dry standing on one edge. A board that has gone grey and rough can be rubbed smooth again with fine sandpaper and a little cooking oil.

Jam sets when it reaches the right temperature, and a cold saucer shows when. Put a spoonful on the saucer, wait a minute and push it with a finger. If the surface wrinkles, the jam is ready to pour into warm jars.

Sunday afternoons at the boating lake follow a pattern. The rowing boats go out first, then the pedal boats, and by four o'clock there is a queue at the kiosk for ice cream that reaches the willow tree.
A torch belongs beside the fuse box, where it can be found in the dark.

The recycling lorry comes every second Wednesday. Glass goes in the green crate, paper in the blue sack, and tins and plastic bottles in the yellow one. Crates put out after seven in the morning are often missed, and the next collection is two weeks away.

Hedgehogs wake from their winter sleep in March and are hungry at once. A shallow dish of water helps them more than food does, and a gap the size of a fist under the garden fence lets them reach the next garden.
A cast iron pan should never soak in the sink. Wipe it out while it is still warm, rinse it briefly, dry it on the hob and rub in a few drops of oil before putting it away.
Fog settles in the valley on still autumn mornings and lifts at about ten. Drivers on the upper road look down on a white lake with only the church tower and the grain silo standing out of it.
Buttons are sewn on with a matchstick underneath, so the thread leaves room for the cloth.

The dentist's waiting room has the same three magazines it had last year. Regular patients bring their own book and arrive exactly on time, since the appointments before lunch tend to run twenty minutes late.

Bulbs for spring are planted in October, three times as deep as the bulb is tall. Daffodils go in clumps of seven or nine, tulips in rows, and crocuses are simply thrown across the lawn and planted where they land.
Milk boils over at the very moment you look away from the pan to answer the door.
A neighbour's parcel taken in on Monday should be handed over by Wednesday. After that it becomes awkward for both sides, and by Friday someone ends up writing a note.

Bath water for a baby should feel neither warm nor cool on the inside of the wrist. Fill the tub only a hand deep, keep one arm behind the child's shoulders the whole time and have the towel within reach before you begin, because there will be no free hand to fetch it later.
The village hall can be booked for birthdays at a small fee. The price includes forty chairs, six trestle tables and the use of the kitchen, but not the cleaning afterwards.
Snow that falls on dry, frozen ground stays. Snow that falls on wet ground melts from below, and by noon the paths are clear while the lawns are still white.
The last bus leaves the market square at twenty to midnight and does not wait.

To descale a kettle, fill it halfway with equal parts of water and vinegar, bring it to the boil and leave it for an hour. Pour the liquid away, rinse twice and boil one full kettle of clean water before making tea again.
Swifts return to the same roof in the first week of May. They stay for barely three months, raise one brood under the tiles and leave again at the start of August, long before the swallows.
The Saturday queue at the bakery moves quickly because everyone knows what they want. Visitors who ask what is in each roll are forgiven, but only once.
Herbs on the windowsill lean towards the glass and need turning every few days.

A new pair of walking boots should be worn around the house for a week before the first long walk. Thick socks, a short route on the first day and a strip of plaster on each heel prevent most blisters. Boots that still rub after a month will probably always rub.

The tide table hangs on a nail inside the door of the beach cafe. The causeway to the island is open for three hours on either side of low water, and the cafe owner will tell anyone who asks how long they have left.
Teaspoons vanish from shared kitchens at a steady rate that nobody has ever explained.

Marmalade oranges appear in the shops for only a few weeks after the new year. They are too bitter to eat raw, which is exactly why they are wanted: the peel and the pips give the preserve its set and its bite.

The night before the bins are emptied, the street fills with the sound of wheels on paving. One household puts its bin out, the next hears it and follows, and within half an hour the whole row is done without a word being said.
Wooden chopping boards are scrubbed with hot water and salt, then stood on edge to dry. Lying flat, a damp board warps.
A spare house key is safest with a neighbour and least safe under the flowerpot.

Porridge is made with one part oats to three parts liquid and a pinch of salt. Stir it over a low heat for five minutes and let it stand for two. Whether the liquid should be milk or water is a question that has divided breakfast tables for generations and will not be settled here.
At the open air pool the water is warmest in late afternoon and the lanes are emptiest just before closing. Season ticket holders swim their lengths then and have the showers to themselves.
Moths are kept out of a wardrobe by clean clothes and moving air, not by scent alone. Wash or brush woollens before storing them, and open the doors wide once a week.
The ferry runs every half hour in summer and hourly from October to Easter.

A bird table brings sparrows first, then tits, and after a week or two a robin that chases the others off. Put out seed in the morning, clear away what is left at dusk and keep the table more than a cat's jump from any fence.
Dusting starts at the top of the room and works down. Lampshades and shelves come first, skirting boards last, and the floor is swept only when everything above it has been done.

Thunder that follows lightning by three seconds is about one kilometre away. When the gap shrinks to nothing it is time to be indoors, away from the windows, with the aerial cable pulled out of the wall.
Lemon juice stops sliced apples from turning brown and keeps a fruit salad fresh until evening.

The allotment society holds its plant sale on the second Sunday in May. Tomato seedlings sell out within the hour, courgettes linger until the afternoon, and whatever is left at four o'clock is given away to anyone still standing near the gate.
Ironing a shirt goes fastest in a fixed order: collar, cuffs, sleeves, then the front panels and finally the back. The shirt should still be slightly damp. A dry shirt needs steam and twice the time.
The waiting time at the level crossing is ninety seconds for a local train and nearly four minutes for a goods train. Cyclists learn to tell the two apart by the sound of the horn.
Fresh paint smells for three days, or longer if the windows stay shut.

A picnic needs less than people pack. Bread, something to put on it, fruit that does not bruise, water and a knife are enough. The blanket matters more than the food, and a spot with afternoon shade matters more than the view.

Garden tools last for decades if they are cleaned before they are put away. Knock the soil off the spade, wipe the blade with an oily rag and hang it up by the handle. A spade left standing in wet earth over winter rusts through at the neck.
The town clock runs four minutes fast and has done so for as long as anyone can remember. People set their watches by the radio and use the clock only to know that they are late.
Ripe pears give slightly when pressed near the stalk and bruise by the next morning.

Hanging a picture needs two people, one to hold it and one to stand back. Mark the top edge lightly in pencil, measure down to where the wire will pull tight and put the nail there. The usual mistake is hanging pictures too high: the middle should sit at eye level for someone standing.
